title: Exponents and the 21 game
summary: Count switch patterns with exponents straight off the breadboard, then hunt the 21 game's doomed spots backwards until the pattern falls out and no grown-up can beat you.
materials: the breadboard with buttons from Build

problems.prompt: Keep the chain going: 3, 6, 12, 24. What comes next?
explanation: Find the rule: compare each number with the one before it.
3 becomes 6, 6 becomes 12, 12 becomes 24: every number is the one before it, doubled.
Double 24 to get 48.
problems.useAgain: when a chain of numbers grows the same way at every step and you need the next one.
hints: Compare each number with the one just before it. What one move turns 3 into 6, and 6 into 12?
The move is the same every time, so do it once more to 24.
problems.socraticHint: What single question could you ask about any two neighbours in this chain to catch its rule?

variant.prompt: Keep the chain going: 5, 10, 20, 40. What comes next?

problems.prompt: A number was doubled three times and landed on 24. What number did it start as?
explanation: Work backwards: doubling forwards means halving backwards.
Walk back from 24 one halving at a time: 24 becomes 12, 12 becomes 6, 6 becomes 3.
Three halvings undo three doublings, so the start was 3. Check forwards: 3, 6, 12, 24.
problems.useAgain: when you know where a chain of steps ended and need to find where it began.
hints: Doubling forwards means halving backwards.
Walk back from 24, one halving at a time, exactly three steps.
problems.socraticHint: If doubling is the forward step, what is the exact undo step, and how many times must you use it?

variant.prompt: A number was doubled twice and landed on 20. What number did it start as?

problems.prompt: In your head: 999 + 456. Use a friendly thousand.
explanation: Guess and round: trade 999 for the friendly 1000.
1000 + 456 is 1456, done in a blink.
You gave the sum 1 too many, so take 1 back: 1455.
problems.useAgain: when a number sits just next to a friendly round one, so you compute with the friendly one and repay the difference.
hints: 999 is one step away from a much friendlier number.
If you add with 1000 instead of 999, is your total too big or too small, and by how much?
problems.socraticHint: Why is adding 1000 and fixing it afterwards faster than adding 999 head-on?

variant.prompt: In your head: 998 + 321. Use a friendly thousand.

problems.prompt: A light starts on. A switch flips it once every second: after 1 second it is off, after 2 seconds on again, and so on. True or false: after 10 seconds the light is back on.
explanation: Find the rule: two flips in a row always bring the light back to where it was.
After 10 seconds the switch has flipped 10 times, and 10 is an even number: five pairs of flips.
Each pair undoes itself, so the light ends exactly where it started: on.
problems.useAgain: when something toggles back and forth and only the even-or-odd count of toggles matters.
hints: Follow the first few seconds with your finger: on, off, on, off. Which seconds leave it on?
Count the flips, then ask whether that count is even or odd.
problems.socraticHint: What do two flips in a row always do to the light, no matter when they happen?

variant.prompt: A light starts on. A switch flips it once every second. True or false: after 7 seconds the light is on.

problem.prompt: Write a capital M on paper, then turn the whole paper upside down, a full half turn. Which letter do you see now?
explanation: Turn it in your head: spin the whole page half a circle, do not mirror it.
The letter M stands on two legs, with a dip hanging down from the top between them.
After a half turn, the top edge becomes the bottom edge: the two legs now point up, and the dip pokes up in the middle.
Two points rising with a valley between them reads as the letter W. The word MOM turning into WOW upside down is this same trick.
problem.useAgain: when a letter, shape or object is turned all the way around and you need to picture where each part ends up.
hints: Do not think of a mirror flip, think of spinning the whole page in a half circle.
Picture where the two legs of the M end up after the spin, and which way the middle dip points.
problem.socraticHint: If you actually spun the paper a half turn on your desk, would what you picture in your head match what the paper shows?

figure.alt: The letter M, written upright, with a half turn shown by a curved arrow. The letter after the turn is not shown.

variant.prompt: Write a capital W on paper, then turn the whole paper upside down, a full half turn. Which letter do you see now?

figure.alt: The letter W, written upright, with a half turn shown by a curved arrow. The letter after the turn is not shown.

problems.prompt: The badge's status strip has 5 plain LEDs, each either on or off, plus one special mode LED that can show red, green or amber instead of just on or off. How many different total displays can the strip show?
explanation: Exponents fast forward: the 5 plain LEDs alone would make 2 to the power 5 patterns, which is 32.
The status LED is not on or off. It has 3 separate states, so each of the 32 patterns can pair with any of them.
Choices stack: 32 patterns times 3 status colors is 96 total displays.
Treating the status LED as just another on or off bit would undercount, since it truly has 3 choices, not 2.
problems.useAgain: when a fast-forward count of choices meets one part of the setup with more than two states.
hints: Work out the plain on or off LEDs first, then ask what the status LED adds on top of that.
The status light does not just double the count the way a plain LED would. How many choices does it really offer?
problems.socraticHint: Why can't the status LED be treated the same way as the other five?

variant.prompt: A second badge has 4 plain LEDs, each either on or off, plus one special mode LED that can show any of 4 colors. How many different total displays can it show?

problems.prompt: Three of these expressions equal the same number. One is an impostor. Which one?
options: 2 to the power 3 + 1 to the power 3
explanation: Do the inside first: work out 2 + 1 before raising it to a power.
(2 + 1) to the power 3 becomes 3 to the power 3, which is 27, and the plain number 27 obviously matches too.
2 to the power 3 + 1 to the power 3 is 8 + 1, which is 9, not 27.
Raising a sum to a power is not the same as raising each part and adding: the parentheses must be done first.
problems.useAgain: when an expression raises a sum to a power and you must check whether splitting it apart first would change the answer.
hints: Work out each expression fully to a plain number before comparing anything.
For the expression with two separate powers added together, do each power first, then add; do not add first.
problems.socraticHint: Does raising a sum to a power give the same answer as raising each piece separately and then adding?

variant.prompt: Three of these expressions equal the same number. One is an impostor. Which one?
options: 3 to the power 3 + 1 to the power 3

problems.prompt: One switch makes 2 patterns, and each extra switch doubles the count. How many patterns do 5 switches make?
explanation: Exponents fast forward: five doublings is 2 to the power 5, five 2s multiplied together.
Climb the chain one switch at a time: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32.
Writing 2 to the power 5 says that whole climb in one breath.
problems.useAgain: when repeated doubling needs counting and you would rather jump straight to the power.
hints: Write the chain out one switch at a time: 2, then 4, then keep going.
You need five numbers in the chain, one for each switch.
problems.socraticHint: How many times does the number 2 get used when you count the patterns of 5 switches this way?

variant.prompt: One switch makes 2 patterns, and each extra switch doubles the count. How many patterns do 6 switches make?

problems.prompt: Which of these equals 2 + 3 to the power 2?
explanation: Do the inside first: powers come before plus, and the little raised 2 belongs to the 3 alone, not to 2 + 3.
3 to the power 2 is 9.
2 + 9 is 11. Adding first and squaring the 5 gives 25, the classic trap.
problems.useAgain: when an expression mixes an exponent with adding or subtracting and the order decides everything.
hints: Ask which number the little raised 2 actually belongs to.
Settle the power completely before any adding happens.
problems.socraticHint: How would the answer change if the problem were written with a bracket, as (2 + 3) to the power 2? Why does that bracket matter so much?

variant.prompt: Which of these equals 20 minus 4 to the power 2?

problems.prompt: Work out 3 times 2 to the power 3.
explanation: Do the inside first: the power belongs to the 2 alone, not to 3 times 2.
2 to the power 3 is 8.
3 times 8 is 24. Multiplying first and cubing the 6 would give 216, a very different animal.
problems.useAgain: when a times sign and an exponent share an expression and the exponent must be settled first.
hints: Which number is being raised to the power 3, the 2 or the 6?
Finish the power completely, then bring in the times 3.
problems.socraticHint: How could you rewrite this with a bracket so nobody could possibly misread it?

variant.prompt: Work out 2 times 3 to the power 2.

problems.prompt:
Tomas counted the blocks in a cube built 6 blocks wide, 6 blocks deep and 6 blocks tall.
Line 1: The cube has 6 blocks along each edge.
Line 2: The total count is 6 multiplied by itself 3 times, written 6 to the power 3.
Line 3: 6 to the power 3 means 6 x 6 x 6, which is 18.
Line 4: So the cube holds 18 blocks in all.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Lines 1 and 2 are correct: with 6 blocks along each edge, the total is 6 to the power 3.
Line 3 is wrong: 6 x 6 x 6 is not 18. Multiplying 6 by itself three times gives 216, not adding 6 three times.
Line 4 then inherited the wrong number: the cube actually holds 216 blocks.
Exponents fast forward: 6 to the power 3 means three copies of 6 multiplied together, never 6 times 3.
problems.useAgain: when an exponent's value needs checking by hand instead of trusting a quick multiplication.
hints: Do not assume any line is correct just because the ones before it look fine. Recompute each line's numbers yourself.
Exponents fast forward: the exponent says exactly how many copies of the base to multiply together, matching the number of dimensions in the cube.
problems.socraticHint: Is 6 to the power 3 the same as 6 times 3, or something else entirely?

variant.prompt:
Priyanka counted the blocks in a cube built 3 blocks wide, 3 blocks deep and 3 blocks tall.
Line 1: The cube has 3 blocks along each edge.
Line 2: Exponents fast forward: multiply 3 by itself once for width, once for depth, once for height, plus one more time to be safe, which is 3 to the power 4.
Line 3: 3 to the power 4 means 3 x 3 x 3 x 3, which works out to 81.
Line 4: So the cube holds 81 blocks in all.
Which line is wrong?

problems.prompt: A hallway wall has a row of 10 light switches. How many different on-off patterns can the whole row show?
explanation: Exponents fast forward: each switch doubles the count, so ten switches make 2 to the power 10 patterns.
Ten little switches hide more than a thousand patterns. This runaway growth is exactly why an exponent feels like a fast forward button.
problems.useAgain: when each new choice doubles the possibilities and the total runs away faster than it looks.
hints: This is the button-pattern count again, just with more switches.
Write the doubling chain and stop at the tenth number.
problems.socraticHint: Before computing anything, would you bet the answer is closer to 20, 200 or 1000? What makes doubling so sneaky to guess about?

variant.prompt: A row has 8 light switches. How many different on-off patterns can the whole row show?

problems.prompt: Which is bigger: 2 to the power 3 plus 2 to the power 3, or 2 to the power 6?
options: 2 to the power 3 plus 2 to the power 3 is bigger
explanation: 2 to the power 3 plus 2 to the power 3 is 8 plus 8, which is 16.
2 to the power 6 means six 2s multiplied together, which is 64.
Adding two equal powers only doubles the value; it does not add their exponents together.
So 2 to the power 6 is bigger, 64 against 16.
problems.useAgain: when two equal powers are added and it is tempting to combine their exponents instead of just doubling the value.
hints: Work each side out to a plain number before comparing them.
Adding two copies of the same power is not the same move as combining their exponents.
problems.socraticHint: If doubling a power does not change its exponent, what does it actually do to the value?

variant.prompt: Which is bigger: 3 to the power 2 plus 3 to the power 2, or 3 to the power 4?
options: 3 to the power 2 plus 3 to the power 2 is bigger

steps.title: Angles measured and reasoned, and every way a roll and a flip can land

problems.prompt: Two angles sit side by side on a straight line. You measure one with a protractor: 65 degrees. What is the other angle, in degrees?
explanation: Angles that sit side by side on a straight line always add up to 180 degrees.
Subtract the angle you measured from 180: 180 minus 65.
180 minus 65 is 115 degrees.
problems.useAgain: when two angles share a straight line and one of them is already measured.
hints: What do two angles on a straight line always add up to?
Subtract the measured angle from that total.
problems.socraticHint: If a straight line is really just a stretched-out straight angle, how many degrees does it always hold?

variant.prompt: Two angles sit side by side on a straight line. You measure one with a protractor: 110 degrees. What is the other angle, in degrees?

problems.prompt: A triangle has two angles measuring 50 degrees and 65 degrees. What is the third angle, in degrees?
explanation: A triangle's three angles always add up to 180 degrees.
Add the two known angles: 50 plus 65 is 115.
Subtract from 180: 180 minus 115 is 65 degrees.
problems.useAgain: when two of a triangle's three angles are known and the third is missing.
hints: What do all three angles of any triangle add up to?
Add the two known angles, then subtract that from 180.
problems.socraticHint: If you tore off all three corners of a triangle and lined them up, what straight shape would they always make?

variant.prompt: A triangle has two angles measuring 40 degrees and 95 degrees. What is the third angle, in degrees?

problems.prompt: You roll one die and flip one coin. How many different outcomes are possible in total?
explanation: The die has 6 faces and the coin has 2 sides, and every face can pair with every side.
Multiply the two counts: 6 times 2.
6 times 2 is 12 different outcomes.
problems.useAgain: when two separate random things happen together, and every result of one can pair with every result of the other.
hints: How many results does the die alone have, and how many does the coin alone have?
Multiply those two counts together.
problems.socraticHint: Does flipping the coin change which numbers the die could show?

variant.prompt: You spin a 4-section spinner and flip one coin. How many different outcomes are possible in total?

problems.prompt: Using that same die and coin, what is the probability, as a fraction in lowest terms, of rolling an even number and flipping heads?
explanation: 3 of the 6 faces are even, and 1 of the 2 coin sides is heads, so 3 times 1 is 3 outcomes you want.
Out of the 12 total outcomes, 3 out of 12 simplifies to 1/4.
problems.useAgain: when a probability question combines two separate random things, and you count the outcomes you want out of all of them.
hints: How many of the 12 total outcomes have both an even number and heads?
Write that count over the total, then simplify the fraction.
problems.socraticHint: Out of all the outcomes you listed, how many of them satisfy both conditions at once?

variant.prompt: Using that same die and coin, what is the probability, as a fraction in lowest terms, of rolling a 6 and flipping tails?

steps.title: The 21 game: hunt the doomed spots

problems.prompt: The 21 game: two players take turns removing 1, 2 or 3 counters from a pile, and whoever takes the last counter wins. It is your turn and 3 counters are left. True or false: you can take the last counter on this very turn.
explanation: The hunt for winning spots starts at the very end of the game, with tiny piles.
The rules let you take up to 3 counters in one turn, and exactly 3 are left.
Take all 3 in one scoop: the last counter is yours and the game is over. Piles of 1, 2 or 3 are all instant wins for the player facing them.
problems.useAgain: when a game looks big and the smart first move is to understand its tiny endings first.
hints: Read the rule again: how many counters may you take in one turn?
Compare the biggest allowed take with the size of the pile in front of you.
problems.socraticHint: From which pile sizes can a player finish the whole game in a single turn?

variant.prompt: Same rules: take 1, 2 or 3, last counter wins. It is your turn and 5 counters are left. True or false: you can take the last counter on this very turn.

problems.prompt: The 21 game again: take 1, 2 or 3 each turn, last counter wins. It is your turn, 4 counters are left, and your opponent plays their best. True or false: no matter what you do, your opponent wins.
explanation: Follow every choice you have, one at a time. Take 1 and you leave 3: your opponent scoops all 3 and wins. Take 2 and you leave 2: scooped. Take 3 and you leave 1: scooped.
Every road out of 4 hands your opponent the win, so 4 is a doomed spot for whoever must move from it.
Now flip it around, because this is the week's big idea: a winning position is a spot from which correct play always wins. If your move can hand your opponent a pile of 4, you are standing in one.
Labeling spots doomed or winning, working backwards from the end of the game, is the master key to every game like this.
problems.useAgain: when you want to know if a game spot is safe, so you label spots from the end backwards instead of guessing forwards.
hints: You have exactly three possible moves from 4. Follow each one to the end of the game.
After each move of yours, count what is left and remember what a pile of 3 or fewer means for the player who faces it.
problems.socraticHint: What is true about all three piles you could leave behind from 4, seen from your opponent's side of the table?

variant.prompt: Same rules: take 1, 2 or 3, last counter wins. It is your turn, 2 counters are left, and your opponent plays their best. True or false: no matter what you do, your opponent wins.

problems.prompt: Take 1, 2 or 3, last counter wins. It is your turn and 6 counters are left. How many should you take?
explanation: A pile of 4 is a doomed spot: whoever must move from it loses to sharp play.
So aim your move at leaving exactly 4. From 6, taking 2 leaves 4.
Then whatever your opponent takes from 4, what remains is 3 or fewer on your turn, and you scoop the last counter.
problems.useAgain: when you know a game's doomed spots and steer every move to park your opponent on one.
hints: You already know one doomed pile size that is smaller than 6.
Ask what take turns 6 into exactly that doomed pile.
problems.socraticHint: You cannot win on this turn. What is the best thing your move can do to the pile instead?

variant.prompt: Take 1, 2 or 3, last counter wins. It is your turn and 7 counters are left. How many should you take?

problems.prompt: In the 21 game, 4 is a doomed spot and so is 8: whoever must move from them loses to sharp play. Keep working backwards. What is the next doomed spot after 8?
explanation: Work backwards: a spot is doomed when every allowed move hands the other player a winning spot.
From 9, 10 or 11 you can reach 8 with one legal take, so all three are winning spots. Dump your opponent on 8 and cruise.
From 12, taking 1, 2 or 3 leaves 11, 10 or 9, all winning spots for your opponent, and 8 is out of reach. So 12 is doomed.
The doomed spots are marching in steps of 4: 4, 8, 12, and the pattern keeps going.
problems.useAgain: when each new answer is built from the answers you already pinned down, so you march step by step from the end.
hints: Check the numbers just above 8 one at a time: from 9, can you dump your opponent on 8?
You are hunting the first number from which 8 cannot be reached in one legal take.
problems.socraticHint: Why must the next doomed spot be more than 3 counters above the last one?

variant.prompt: The doomed spots found so far are 4, 8 and 12. Working backwards the same way, what is the next doomed spot after 12?

problems.prompt: The real thing: the pile starts at 21 and you go first. Take 1, 2 or 3, last counter wins. How many do you take?
explanation: The doomed spots are the multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20.
Your first move should park your opponent on one. From 21, taking 1 leaves exactly 20.
From then on, whatever they take, you take enough to make your two moves add up to 4 together. The pile walks down 20, 16, 12, 8, 4, 0, and the counter that makes it 0 lands in your hand.
problems.useAgain: when a game's whole strategy collapses into one question: which doomed spot can I reach from here?
hints: First list the doomed spots from 4 up past 20.
Find the one doomed spot you can reach from 21 with a single legal take.
problems.socraticHint: Out of all the doomed spots on your list, which one can your very first move actually reach, and why is it the only one in reach?

variant.prompt: The pile starts at 18 and you go first. Take 1, 2 or 3, last counter wins. How many do you take?

problems.prompt: Two players who both know the whole secret sit down to play. Take 1, 2 or 3, last counter wins, and the pile starts at 16. True or false: the player who goes second can always win.
explanation: 16 is a multiple of 4, a doomed spot, and it is the first player who must move from it.
Whatever the first player takes, the second player tops it up to 4 in total. A take of 1 is answered with 3, a take of 2 with 2, a take of 3 with 1.
After every second-player move the pile sits on a multiple of 4 again, stepping 16, 12, 8, 4, 0 down the line. The counter that makes it 0 belongs to the second player.
At a pile of 16, the generous-looking offer of the first move is actually the winning move.
problems.useAgain: when going first is not automatically best and one fact about the starting number decides which seat holds the win.
hints: Check whether the starting pile is itself a doomed spot, then ask which player is standing on it.
The second player never chooses alone: their take answers the first player's take.
problems.socraticHint: In this game, is moving first a prize or a burden? What single fact about the starting number settles it?

variant.prompt: Same two players, same rules, and the pile starts at 17. True or false: the player who goes second can always win.

problems.prompt: Write the whole secret down for a friend: in the 21 game, why does leaving your opponent a pile that is a multiple of 4 win you the game every time, no matter how they play?
explanation: Start at the very end: 0 is a multiple of 4 too. Facing an empty pile means the last counter is already gone, taken by you.
From any multiple of 4, your opponent must take 1, 2 or 3, so they can never land on the next multiple of 4 themselves. They always stop short of it.
Whatever they take, you take the rest of 4: their 1 meets your 3, their 2 your 2, their 3 your 1 in reply. Together one round always removes exactly 4, multiple to multiple.
So the pile steps down 20, 16, 12, 8, 4, 0, landing on a multiple of 4 after every move of yours. The step onto 0, the last counter, is always yours.
problems.useAgain: when a winning trick works once and you want to show it must keep working all the way to the end of the game.
hints: Start from the end: what does an empty pile mean, and for which player?
Think in rounds of two moves, theirs plus yours, and ask what the two takes can always add up to.
problems.socraticHint: Your opponent's take is out of your control. What can you still control about the total the two of you remove together in one round?

steps.title: Explain it in writing
steps.prompt: Write why taking 1 from the opening pile of 21 is the only first move that cannot lose, one idea per sentence. Name the idea you used.

steps.title: Explain back
steps.prompt: Play the real 21 game against a grown-up tonight, counters on the table, best of three. After that, challenge the AI too: a grown-up opens the chat, you type in the rules of the 21 game, then play it move by move and watch whether it ever parks you on a doomed spot. Then record yourself explaining the trick as if to a friend: the doomed spots, and how you kept parking your opponents on them.

extras.title: How your brain keeps this
extras.body:
Before the season starts, ten minutes on how your own brain keeps things. Everything in this app is built on it.

1. Reading something again feels like learning. It mostly is not. Pulling it back out of your head, without looking, is what makes it stay. That is why the mistake box brings a problem back weeks later in a new shape.
2. The gap matters. A thing you meet in week 3 and again in week 7 sticks far better than a thing you meet twice in one afternoon. The warm-ups do this on purpose.
3. Sleep is when the day's learning gets filed. A hard bar practised before bed is easier in the morning for a reason.
4. A mistake is data, not a mark against you. Finding out you were sure and wrong is the most useful moment of the week. That is why the app asks what made it feel certain.
5. Small and often beats long and rare. Four sittings of fifteen minutes teach more than one hour, in music and in math alike.

Now write one goal for this season in your own words in this week's Maker's Log. Make it something you will be able to do in week 12 that you cannot do today. At the last Showcase you read it back.

What to notice: which of the five you already do without being told, and which one you have been avoiding.
